To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1), SLE patients spontaneously produce ANA in vitro but normal controls rarely do; (2) T cells are required for ANA production; (3) ANA production is triggered by soluble factors produced in the culture supernatant; (4) the factors are not specific for the SLE patients; (5) the factors are heat stable and are not absorbed by the anti-DNA antibodies.

SLE patients spontaneously produce anti-nuclear antibodies in unstimulated peripheral blood mononucleocytes, whereas normal individuals rarely do; autoreactive clones are present in normal individuals but kept under control and T cell help is needed for anti-nuclear antibody triggering.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of autoimmunity in SLE and the role of the T cell in the triggering of ANA.
the in vitro production and characterization of ANA in SLE.
a new mechanism for autoimmunity, namely, the induction of autoreactive B cell clones to produce ANA by T cell help and a soluble factor(s) produced by SLE patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the in vitro induction of ANA in PBMC from SLE patients is a complex process involving T cells and a soluble factor(s) in PBMC supernatant.
SLE patients have a defect in T cell control of B cells.
the T cell requirement is a general feature of the production of ANA in vitro, but the nature of the inducing factors and the mechanism of the induction are still unknown.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ANA triggering in vitro is a complex phenomenon requiring both T and B cells, as well as a soluble factor(s).
the production of ANA in vitro in the absence of antigenic stimulation is a characteristic of SLE patients.
the autoreactive B cell clones in SLE are activated by T cells which are activated by a soluble factor(s) produced by SLE monocytes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SLE patients spontaneously produce anti-nuclear antibodies in vitro, while normal individuals rarely do.

the presence of ANA in the serum of patients does not always reflect the presence of autoreactive B cells in the peripheral blood, but that the presence of autologous T cells and soluble factor(s) may be required for the triggering of ANA production.
the production of ANA is a T cell-dependent process in SLE patients.
